RagShortTexts: Mongol forces overcame resistance at Kolomna in 1238 during the invasion of northeastern Rus.
Kolomna’s position near the Moskva–Oka junction mattered for movement and retreat.

Variants.Content: In 1238 Mongol forces advancing through northeastern Rus defeated resistance near Kolomna. The town lay close to the meeting of the Moskva and Oka, where men arriving from different directions had to find one another before access to rivers could become effective assistance. The defeat did not halt the invaders; other towns still faced attack and displacement. Princely messengers sought news of retainers, while residents along the roads recognised danger through lost livestock, retreating men and families seeking shelter.

Assembly near a junction requires knowledge of which bank an ally holds, available boats and responsibility for messages. Kolomna gives lords reason to distinguish provisions for a garrison from those needed by men meeting the enemy outside.

Winter routes carry armies as well as scouts and can obscure an enemy’s direction. Memories of Kolomna prompt questions about regrouping and recovering companions after horses are lost, rather than assuming a river alone prevents approach.

Villages receiving defeated men and displaced families also consume stores. Giving away the last working animal jeopardises sowing. Residents remember who provided a recognised guarantee as well as those who simply took provisions.
